analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Clean Air Act rules that cut power plant pollution causing acid rain.
analysis.headline: The bill to wipe out the Clean Air Act's acid rain controls, introduced by Rep. Tom DeLay with one cosponsor, never got a vote: it sat in a House committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have deleted Title IV of the Clean Air Act, the section that limits the sulfur and nitrogen pollution from power plants that causes acid rain. Repealing it would have freed coal-burning utilities from those emission limits entirely. It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and never moved, so the pollution rules stayed on the books.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of coal-fired power plants, especially those burning high-sulfur coal, would have been freed from the sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide limits, allowance requirements, and compliance costs of the acid rain program. High-sulfur coal mining companies would also have gained back demand that the rules had pushed plants away from.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Title IV of the Clean Air Act outright, eliminating the acid deposition control program — the emission caps on sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide from power plants and the allowance system used to meet them.

With those limits gone, utilities would no longer bear the cost of cutting acid-rain-causing emissions or trading allowances, and plants would be free to burn cheaper high-sulfur coal without penalty.

analysis.who_pays: The public would pay in pollution: more acid rain damaging lakes, forests, and buildings, and more sulfur-based fine particle pollution in the air people breathe. Low-sulfur coal producers, who had gained business because the rules pushed plants toward cleaner coal, would lose demand. Regions downwind of midwestern power plants would bear most of it.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Title IV would have removed the emission controls that curb acid rain and the sulfur fine-particle pollution linked to respiratory illness, shifting the cost of dirty air onto the public's health and onto ecosystems.

The strongest good-faith case for repeal was that the acid rain rules imposed real compliance costs on utilities and squeezed demand for high-sulfur coal, affecting coalfield communities; the bill offered no replacement program or transition help — it simply deleted the rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings in this bill flow to utilities and high-sulfur coal interests, while the cost — renewed acid rain and more particulate air pollution — falls on everyone downwind. There is no offsetting public benefit in the bill: it is a straight deletion of the pollution limits, with no transition assistance for coal communities and no alternative program. Weighed honestly, the public cost would have outweighed the concentrated private gain.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power and Health and Environment subcommittees, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom DeLay introduced the bill on January 11, 1995, to repeal Title IV of the Clean Air Act, the acid deposition control program.
It drew a single Republican cosponsor and was referred to the House Committee on Commerce.
In February 1995 it was sent to the Energy and Power and Health and Environment subcommittees, and no further action was ever taken — no markup, no floor vote, nothing in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people downwind of coal plants and the regions with acid-damaged lakes and forests: the acid rain rules stayed in force because repeal never came close to a vote. Utilities and high-sulfur coal producers got no relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Clean air rules survived; utilities got nothing

for.name: Rep. Tom DeLay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Clean Air Act's acid rain title on January 11, 1995.

for.name: One House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members signed on.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Thomas J. Bliley Jr.)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never brought the bill to a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republicans ever attached their names — a sponsor and one cosponsor — and no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call pattern exists.

industries.note: Title IV caps each plant's sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions and requires allowances to cover them; repeal would have erased those obligations and their compliance costs. The utilities' gain would come directly as more acid rain and sulfate air pollution for the public.

The acid rain program pushed power plants toward low-sulfur coal and scrubbers, cutting demand for high-sulfur coal. Repeal would have revived that demand, but at the cost of the emissions causing acid rain.
Western and other low-sulfur coal producers gained customers because the rules made cleaner coal cheaper to burn than adding controls. Repealing the rules would have taken that demand away.
